Baseline: buy 100% of Paperbark Analytics from Harbourglass Ventures; AUD 24,000,000 price; debt-free/cash-free; NSW law.

=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.
exchanges.text:
## Buyer’s position

**Do not accept this package as “FINAL”.** The Seller’s assertion that the terms are market-standard or agreed at principal level is not evidence of Buyer approval. Confirm any actual approvals with Wattlebridge’s deal team. Market ranges alone do not establish an acceptable allocation of these transaction-specific risks.

The central concern is the **combined effect** of the drafting: blanket disclosure and constructive Buyer knowledge could defeat claims before the low cap, thresholds and short time limits even apply. Extending that regime to title, tax, indemnities and completion obligations materially compounds the problem.

This review is based on the supplied extracts, not the complete SPA or underlying DD documents.

## 1. Completion and price protection: highest-priority pushbacks

| Issue | Buyer concern and reasoning | Recommended position |
|---|---|---|
| **Bluefen consent — clauses 3 / 6.3** | Bluefen represents approximately **30% of FY26 revenue**. Reasonable endeavours do not secure continuity of that revenue. Delivery of a consent document alone is insufficient where clause 11.3 imposes associated conditions. The Disclosure Letter expressly confirms that final consent and evidence of satisfaction are missing. | Require a Buyer-waivable condition precedent for valid, effective written consent **and satisfaction of all associated conditions**, without materially adverse amendments, fees or restrictions unless Buyer approves. Require supporting evidence and an appropriate long-stop/termination mechanism. Do not allow Seller to deem the condition satisfied by delivery alone. |
| **Riverlark debt and security — clauses 2 / 7** | Approximately **AUD 3.2m** remains outstanding. A promise to release security after Completion leaves Buyer owning an indebted, potentially encumbered company and may expose it to change-of-control default. That is inconsistent with the debt-free/cash-free bargain unless properly dealt with in the completion mechanics. | Obtain a binding payoff letter covering principal, interest, fees and break costs, together with lender consent or waiver where needed. Repay through the completion funds flow and obtain effective releases of all relevant security and guarantees at Completion. Later administrative registration of releases is distinguishable from an unsecured promise to procure a release later. |
| **Completion bonuses — AUD 420,000 plus possible on-costs** | The Seller calls these its responsibility, but that label does not prevent the acquired company from bearing the liability. Their omission from the funds flow creates a potential economic shortfall. | Expressly allocate the agreed bonus cost and applicable superannuation, payroll tax and other on-costs to Seller economics. Provide for payment, deduction or a defined transaction-expense/debt-like adjustment, with evidence and a true-up if necessary. Check the continued-employment conditions and avoid double counting in working capital or other adjustments. |
| **Ironquay IP — clause 11.1** | The apparent issue is not merely an **AUD 180,000 invoice**. Transfer of SOW3 Project Materials depends on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. The record neither independently establishes non-payment nor demonstrates that title has passed. An indemnity confined to the invoice does not address missing IP ownership or business disruption. | Verify the full SOW3 payment position and scope of affected materials. Require Seller-funded clearance of any outstanding sums and a confirmatory assignment/release establishing the necessary rights, preferably before Completion. Broaden the indemnity to losses from the identified ownership/payment defect, including relevant third-party claims and remediation costs, rather than only the specified payment. If unresolved, consider a condition, retention or escrow. |

**Funds-flow principle:** reconcile the AUD 24m headline price to actual completion payments and the agreed debt-free/cash-free adjustment mechanism. Seller-funded discharge of liabilities must not quietly become additional Buyer consideration.

## 2. Liability regime: resist applying one narrow remedy to every risk

### General warranty cap: 20% / AUD 4.8m

The arithmetic is correct. A 20% cap is not necessarily unacceptable for ordinary business warranties, but it should be assessed against diligence findings, Seller covenant strength, available insurance and the other limitations.

**Pushback:** treat this as a negotiable cap for **general warranties only**, not the default for all obligations. Known risks need express treatment rather than reliance on a capped general warranty claim.

### De minimis and deductible basket

The AUD 25,000 de minimis and AUD 250,000 deductible basket mean Buyer bears qualifying losses up to the basket and recovers only the excess thereafter. The basket is approximately **1.04% of price**.

**Pushback:**
- Seek lower thresholds and a **tipping basket**, under which qualifying losses are recoverable from the first dollar once the basket is exceeded.
- Aggregate claims arising from the same or related facts so Seller cannot fragment one problem into sub-threshold claims.
- Exclude fundamental warranties, tax protections, specific indemnities, fraud and payment/adjustment obligations from these thresholds.

These amounts are not automatically objectionable in isolation; their effect becomes more seller-friendly when combined with the disclosure and knowledge provisions.

### General warranty time limit: 18 months

Eighteen months may not capture issues identified through a full audit and reporting cycle.

**Pushback:** seek at least 24 months for general warranties, calibrated to the financial reporting timetable. Review any separate requirement to commence proceedings: timely notice should preserve the claim, with workable notice requirements and suitable treatment of contingent liabilities.

Reject the proposal that limitations apply to **all Claims unless expressly excluded**. Define each protection’s scope affirmatively and check every cross-reference.

### Fundamental/title warranties

“Administrative simplicity” is not a reason for Buyer to bear the risk that Seller lacks authority or cannot transfer the shares.

**Pushback:** separate capacity, authority, title and encumbrance warranties from the general regime; seek a cap of at least **100% of price**, no basket or de minimis, and a substantially longer period aligned with applicable limitation rules. Preserve the obligation to transfer good title itself.

### Tax and IP

Neither should simply be treated as “settled” under the general regime.

- **Tax:** seek a specific covenant/indemnity for agreed pre-Completion tax exposures, alongside tax warranties, with appropriate exclusions to prevent double recovery. Survival should accommodate relevant assessment periods and a claims buffer.
- **IP:** obtain meaningful ownership, licensing, infringement and contractor-chain-of-title warranties, with any separate cap and duration calibrated to the business’s dependence on its IP. The known Ironquay issue needs its own protection regardless.

### All-claims limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance

Clauses 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 could undermine express indemnities, price adjustments, completion covenants and remedies for misleading conduct—not just warranty claims.

**Pushback:** expressly preserve:
- Fraud, fraudulent misrepresentation and deliberate concealment, without indirectly excluding responsibility through an unduly narrow attribution rule.
- Specific indemnities and their separately agreed regimes.
- Price, debt, leakage and adjustment payment obligations.
- Appropriate termination, specific performance and injunctive remedies.
- Rights and liabilities that cannot lawfully be excluded.

Non-reliance and exclusive-remedy language needs NSW-law review. Do not assume that it can validly exclude every statutory claim—or accept it on that basis.

## 3. Disclosure and Buyer knowledge: significant erosion of protection

### Blanket data-room and public-register disclosure

Merely including or referring to information somewhere in a data room should not automatically qualify every warranty. The proposed wording transfers interpretation and discovery risk to Buyer, including where documents are incomplete or inconsistent.

**Pushback:**
- Require **fair disclosure in sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope** of the matter.
- Seek specific linkage to the affected warranties.
- Reject blanket public-record and data-room disclosure, or tightly delimit any agreed exceptions.
- Preserve a fixed, indexed copy of the disclosed materials and a controlled process for later disclosures.
- State that disclosure does not qualify specific indemnities, completion conditions or price adjustments unless expressly agreed.

The 22 September cutoff is also relevant: obtain updated diligence and appropriate signing/Completion confirmations. Seller should not gain an automatic cure of breaches merely by making later disclosure.

### Buyer/adviser knowledge — clause 8.3

“Discoverable” matters create **constructive knowledge**, not actual knowledge. Attributing all advisers’ knowledge to Buyer makes this particularly broad and could defeat claims on the basis that Buyer ought to have found the issue.

**Pushback:** delete the exclusion. If a commercial compromise is required, confine it to actual, conscious knowledge of specifically named Buyer deal-team members at an agreed time, with no imputed adviser knowledge or duty of enquiry. It should not override specific indemnities or agreed risk allocations.

Knowing about a problem does not mean Buyer has agreed to pay for it.

## 4. Other disclosed matters: investigate without overstating the evidence

**Export/privacy incident — DD-006.**  
Seller’s “not expected to be material” description is not established by the preliminary record. Conversely, the record does **not** prove unauthorised access, a notifiable breach or quantified loss.

Require preservation of evidence, investigation of access and scope, containment and remediation, and assessment of applicable privacy, contractual and notification obligations. Consider a tailored pre-Completion incident indemnity and, if material uncertainty persists, retention or a completion condition. Cover agreed investigation, remediation and third-party liabilities, with penalties only to the extent legally indemnifiable. Do not let ordinary warranty disclosure nullify this protection.

**Sandbar renewals — AUD 330,000 aggregate.**  
Assess the three related renewals together for interim-covenant thresholds and commercial exposure. Establish timing, necessity, cancellation rights, accruals and whether Seller entered them with required approval. They are **not automatically debt-like liabilities or extraordinary expenditure** merely because they are disclosed. Seek consent controls over material new commitments and a price adjustment or specific remedy only where the facts and agreed economics support one.

**Office lease — DD-007.**  
The extract identifies a notification obligation, not landlord consent to the share sale. Check the full lease and require timely compliant notice; do not invent a consent condition.

**Mossvale — DD-009.**  
An assignment restriction alone does not establish that a share sale requires consent. Check for separate change-of-control or deemed-assignment language before deciding whether action is necessary.

**Share title — DD-012.**  
The register is relevant evidence, not complete title diligence. Verify issued capital, historic issuances/transfers, options and other rights, constitutional/shareholder restrictions and encumbrances. Require appropriate transfer instruments, approvals, register updates and robust title warranties. Do not concede that Buyer has independently verified title merely because the register was disclosed.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Secure completion deliverables:** effective Bluefen consent and conditions; Riverlark repayment and security releases; satisfactory resolution of Ironquay ownership.
2. **Protect price economics:** expressly allocate bonuses and on-costs, debt discharge and other agreed Seller costs without double counting.
3. **Separate liability categories:** general warranties must not swallow title, tax, specific indemnities, payment obligations or fraud protections.
4. **Reject blanket disclosure and constructive knowledge:** these could otherwise make negotiated warranties largely ineffective.
5. **Resolve factual uncertainty:** investigate the incident and renewals; verify title; distinguish actual consent requirements from notification or assignment provisions.
6. **Check the complete SPA and approvals:** do not accept Seller’s “market”, “agreed” or “FINAL” labels as substitutes for Buyer instructions or operative drafting.
